capabilities.name: Buildkite Integration
capabilities.description: Runs CI on a self-hosted Buildkite agent (Apple silicon) instead of a metered cloud fleet. The pipeline and its GitHub webhook are created during generation, so there is no manual "set up project" step. Can run alongside CircleCI, so a repository can migrate without a flag day.

actions.description: The pipeline is created in the Buildkite organisation during generation
Registers the pipeline GitHub webhook and triggers the first build. Without the webhook, pushes trigger nothing

queue.description: Buildkite agent queue the generated pipeline targets.

provisionPipeline.description: Create the pipeline and register its GitHub webhook during generation. Set to false to only emit the .buildkite/ config.

branchGating.description: Run the heavy gates (Lighthouse, preview deploys) on main only by default. Set to false to run them on every branch.

benefits: Runs on your own hardware — no per-minute metering
No manual setup: the pipeline and its push webhook are provisioned for you
Installs dependencies once per build rather than once per step

capabilities.name: GitHub Releases
capabilities.description: Publishes a GitHub Release with attached artifacts when a version is cut. The release step lives in the Buildkite pipeline, so it runs only after build and test passed on that commit: the version is bumped from the last tag, the tag is created by CI, the artifacts named by the project's own scripts/release-artifacts.sh are attached, and the release is published with generated notes. No version bookkeeping, and no PAT for a human to paste in.

targets.description: Per-target release artifacts, one build per Rust-triple label. Empty means a single artifact for the default target (notes-only when the language has no artifact paths). Labels are the release vocabulary the launcher resolves against, so the pipeline's matrix and the launcher's lookup consume the same table.

benefits: Cutting a version is one click - CI tags, packages and publishes
The release can only exist for a commit that passed build and test in Buildkite
Versions bump from the last tag; no version file to keep in sync
Artifacts are named by scripts/release-artifacts.sh, which regeneration never overwrites

capabilities.name: Fetch and Launch
capabilities.description: Seeds scripts/fetch-launch.sh: a launcher that fetches the newest release for the host, verifies its sha256 against the release manifest, unpacks it and execs it. Fail-open by design - a host never fails to boot because GitHub was unreachable. It consumes the per-target artifacts github-release publishes, so the two are selected together.
benefits: A host starts once and keeps itself on the newest release
The payload is verified against the manifest's sha256 before it becomes current
Fail-open: an unreachable GitHub never stops a host from booting
No daemon, no timer, no rollback - one fetch, one symlink flip, one exec

capabilities.name: Docker Container
capabilities.description: Containerize the project and publish to the GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) for deployment to a NAS or self-hosted host via Docker Compose. Mutually exclusive with other deployment systems.

actions.description: GHCR package is created on first push from CircleCI

Create a classic PAT with the write:packages scope (fine-grained PATs cannot access GHCR); add GHCR_USERNAME and GHCR_TOKEN to the CircleCI context. The generated Dockerfile labels the image with its GitHub repo so GHCR links the package to it (public repo -> public package)

publishPort.description: Compose port binding, e.g. "3000:3000" or "127.0.0.1:3000:3000" for a private (Tailscale-only) service. The left-hand side is the published HOST port — Homepage href/widget URLs use it, so "127.0.0.1:3002:3000" yields http://<hostname>:3002/.

baseImage.description: Runtime base image. Defaults to a glibc image (node:22-slim / python:3.12-slim); Alpine only for pure-JS apps.

hostname.description: Hostname used in the Homepage href (defaults to localhost; set to your NAS hostname/IP for browser access).

registryNamespace.description: GHCR registry namespace (GitHub user/org). Defaults to the authenticated GitHub login at generation time.

dataMounts.description: Host data mounts emitted into compose volumes, e.g. [{ "hostPath": "/volume1/data", "containerPath": "/data", "readOnly": true }]. Read-only by default.

aptPackages.description: Debian packages installed in the runtime image via apt, e.g. ["iproute2", "curl"]. curl is added automatically for Python http healthchecks.

envVars.description: Environment variables emitted into the compose environment and .env.example, e.g. ["MCP_PORT=3001"] (a bare key like "MCP_PORT" is filled from .env).

pythonDependencies.description: Runtime Python dependencies (PEP 508 specifiers) emitted into [project] dependencies of the generated pyproject.toml, e.g. ["mcp>=1.2.0", "mcpo>=0.1.0", "httpx>=0.27.0"]. Empty by default; dev tools (pytest, ruff) live in the dev extra.

command.description: Container CMD override (exec form), e.g. ["/usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh"]. Defaults to a language-appropriate command. A /usr/local/bin/<script> reference is copied from scripts/<script> in the repo (see deploy/README.md).

entrypoint.description: Container ENTRYPOINT override (exec form), e.g. ["/usr/local/bin/entrypoint.sh"]. A /usr/local/bin/<script> reference is copied from scripts/<script> in the repo (see deploy/README.md).

healthcheck.description: Health mechanism: "none", "http:<path>" (e.g. "http:/healthz"; installs curl on Python images), or "command:<cmd>". The Dockerfile HEALTHCHECK and Homepage widget are only emitted when declared. Node web apps default to "http:/health".

language.description: Project language override. Normally derived from the selected devcontainer-* capability; set this only to override it.

armBuilds.description: Also build and publish linux/arm64 images. Defaults to false (x86_64 / linux/amd64 only) — set true when a deploy host (e.g. an ARM NAS or Raspberry Pi) needs arm64 images.

benefits: Deploy to any Docker host (Synology, Unraid, TrueNAS, VPS) — not tied to a cloud vendor
Auto-updates via Watchtower polling the registry
Surfaced in Homepage dashboard with a health widget
Full local/private control of the container

capabilities.name: MicroPython board
capabilities.description: Adds the MicroPython board toolchain (mpremote) plus the USB passthrough plumbing needed to drive an RP2-series board (RP2040 or RP2350) from inside the devcontainer. OrbStack forwards the board's CDC-ACM REPL into the Linux VM automatically, but a container only sees it when the device is granted explicitly - this capability emits that grant and a port auto-detect helper. The container keeps the macOS node name (/dev/tty.usbmodem<serial>), which changes with the USB port, so the port is discovered at runtime. Note the grant is deliberately broad: OrbStack assigns the node a dynamic character major, and the device-cgroup-rule grammar accepts only a single major or '*', so scoping the grant to USB serial is not expressible - the container can open any host character device. Access is exclusive: while the container holds the port, host tools such as Thonny cannot open it.

deviceAccess.description: How the container is granted the serial device. "cgroup-rule" (default, bench-verified) binds the host /dev into the container and allows the whole character-device cgroup class, so the container always starts whether or not the board is attached, and the board is hot-pluggable. It is deliberately not scoped to USB serial: OrbStack assigns a dynamic major and the rule grammar takes only a single major or '*'. "privileged" is the escape hatch, for the case where the cgroup-rule mechanism stops working on a future OrbStack; it grants every device class plus all capabilities, so it is broader than the default on every axis. There is deliberately no pinned-device mode - see the capability spec, section 5.

deviceGlob.description: Pattern used at RUNTIME by scripts/find-board.sh to enumerate candidate ports. OrbStack preserves the macOS node name, so this is the usbmodem form and NOT /dev/ttyACM0. Only change it for a board that enumerates as a generic USB-serial adapter (then it is ttyUSB* on Linux, tty.usbserial* on the macOS side).

board.description: The board/product this repo targets - a NAME, not a chip. Drives the README's product line and firmware-repo pointer. Product and chip are selected on separate axes on purpose: a product can ship with more than one RP2 variant (the Pimoroni Galactic Unicorn has been sold as both an RP2040 and a Pico 2 W / RP2350 carrier), so asserting a chip inside a product label is how the wrong .uf2 gets chosen with no warning. Set `chip` to say which silicon this repo targets.

enumLabels.unknown: Unknown - read the board's runtime banner

chip.description: The RP2 silicon variant this firmware targets, chosen independently of `board`. The MicroPython .uf2 is selected by CHIP, and the RP2040 and RP2350 builds are not interchangeable, so this is the axis a wrong-flash hangs on. Do not guess it from a product name, the purchase date, or the USB PID: `2e8a:0005` identifies the MicroPython CDC firmware class and says nothing about the variant. The one reliable source is the board's runtime banner - `mpremote connect "$(scripts/find-board.sh)" exec 'import os; print(os.uname().machine)'` - and `unknown` makes the generated README say exactly that instead of asserting a chip it cannot know.

packages.description: PyPI packages installed into the devcontainer's Python environment for board work, e.g. ["mpremote", "esptool"]. mpremote is the CLI the whole workflow is built on; the agent-driven iteration loop in the design memo depends on it being scriptable, and find-board.sh uses it to identify which candidate port is the board.

benefits: Drive the board from inside the devcontainer - no host-side toolchain to install or keep in sync
mpremote is scriptable, so an agent can iterate on firmware far faster than clicking in Thonny
The devcontainer opens whether or not the board is attached, and the board is hot-pluggable
The board is identified by probing it rather than by guessing at a port name that changes on every replug
The exclusivity constraint, the breadth of the device grant and the OrbStack forwarding model are all documented in the generated README, not left to be rediscovered
